newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- ECI and Alan Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- ECI and Alan Greenspan.

text.p: The U.S. credit market will focus Tuesday on first-quarter employment costs and a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, analysts said.
The Employment Cost Index (ECI), regarded as one of the most reliable indicators of compensation inflation, should set the day's tone at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Economists in a Reuters poll projected ECI grew 0.9 percent last quarter and 3.1 percent year-on-year. That compares with fourth-quarter readings of up 0.8 percent quarterly and 2.8 percent annually.
"This is an important report because it gives us the best indication about where labor costs are," said Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co.

Market expectations appear tightly wound around economists' consensus forecasts. An ECI level of 1.0 percent or higher would be read bearishly, while relief trade could follow a 0.8- or 0.9-percent reading, analysts said.
Katz explained that the consensus forecast for a 3.1 percent year-on-year ECI gain would not be particularly inflationary.

"While that's a rise from the low point we saw sometime last year, it's still relatively on the low side," Katz said. "It suggests there's been some minor wage creep, but nothing yet to get too worried about with regard to affecting overall inflation."

Besides reacting to the headline ECI number, market players will look closely at individual components within the report. They will examine how much the index rose because of wages/salaries increases and how much of the rise came from benefits costs.

Wages and salaries comprise the largest share of ECI, but their gains have been offset somewhat in recent reports by less-pronounced increases in benefits. Many analysts, however, believe medical care-related inflation may trend higher.

"There's been a lot of chatter, including by the chairman of the Fed, that the improvement in medical care costs is going to bottom out," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.
Within wages and salaries, private industry compensation would warrant a close look, Youngdahl said.
"We want to see if private industry is substantially pushing up the overall level of wages...in an effort to respond to the tightness in the labor market," he said.
The ECI eclipses other economic reports Tuesday, even a couple that occasionally get top-tier billing.
Durable goods orders for March, also set for release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, should be unchanged after rising 1.5 percent in February, economists projected.
"It's kind of overshadowed and that report on a monthly basis is kind of all over the place," said John Park, an economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.

In addition, April Consumer Confidence, expected to read 118.4 after a 118.5 reading in March, is scheduled to be released at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. And the weekly proprietary indexes of retail sales will be released, as well.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan tops Tuesday's list of influential speakers. He addresses the International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Bank spring meeting in Washington at 1230 EDT/1630 GMT.
"He'll probably talk big-picture platitudes. I doubt he'll get pinned down and talk about the money market outlook," said Carey Leahey, senior vice president and senior economist at Lehman Bros.
But Leahey and some other analysts said the central bank chief may comment on the labor market in general and perhaps even the ECI in specific.
Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus and Philadelphia Fed President Boehne also have speaking engagements on Tuesday.
